title: Linear Regression-Based Calibration for a PLC-Controlled 3-DoF Robotic Arm in a Water Treatment Plant

authors.name: Dr. A. R. Nugroho
authors.affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Universitas Gadjah Mada

abstract: Handling chemical materials in water treatment plants (WTPs) requires high positional precision, predictable timing, and deterministic safety interlocks. Conventional PLC-based control of 3-DoF robotic manipulators at municipal WTPs typically relies on nominal encoder mappings and PID compensation, which yields residual positioning errors and suboptimal dosing repeatability. We present a pragmatic implementation of batch linear regression calibration embedded in a PLC-centered control architecture for a 3-DoF robotic arm installed at the Universitas Gadjah Mada WTP testbed. The proposed method reduces end-effector RMSE from 3.60 mm to 1.20 mm and increases dosing positional accuracy from 89.2% to 95.4% while reducing control loop latency from 45.3 ms to 12.3 ms in our hardware-in-the-loop trials. The solution integrates a Siemens S7-1500 PLC, an STM32F407 auxiliary logger, and servo amplifiers with PROFINET communication; regression training uses N=500 samples and executes during off-peak maintenance windows. We discuss tuning tradeoffs, safety integration, scan-cycle impacts ($T_{\mathrm{scan}}$), and deployment limitations for full-scale WTP operations.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Water treatment plants (WTPs) often require automated manipulation for chemical dosing, sensor sampling, and maintenance tasks. Robotic manipulators reduce occupational exposure to hazardous chemicals and increase repeatability of dosing events, which has direct public-health impact. For municipal treatment processes, equipment must comply with industrial control norms such as deterministic scan cycles, fail-safe I/O, and traceable dosing logs. In practice, affordable three degree-of-freedom (3-DoF) arms are attractive because they cover pick, place, and dispense tasks inside chemical dosing bays while remaining mechanically simple enough to integrate with existing PLC infrastructure. Operational reliability at this level matters because dosing errors of a few millimetres translate to concentration deviations downstream and can require manual corrective actions by operators.

Prior efforts addressing robotic calibration and industrial integration include model-based identification, encoder remapping, and closed-loop observers [1][2]. Many academic solutions assume high-performance real-time Linux controllers or dedicated GPUs [3][4], which complicates deployment to PLC-dominant plants. PLC vendors have improved computational capability (e.g., Siemens S7-1500) but ladder logic and IEC 61131-3 function blocks still constrain the range of algorithms that are practical on-device [5]. A practical limitation of prior work is that either the calibration algorithm is too heavy for embedded PLC cycles or the integration with plant safety logic is incomplete, producing risky failure modes when applied to chemical handling tasks [6].

The specific problem addressed in this paper is how to implement a lightweight, certifiable calibration algorithm that operates within the timing and safety constraints of a PLC-based control system while materially improving positional accuracy and dosing repeatability for a 3-DoF arm in a WTP environment. The research gap is concrete: published robotics calibration techniques rarely present end-to-end PLC implementations with measured scan-cycle impacts $T_{\mathrm{scan}}$ and with hardware-in-the-loop results using real dosing hardware and industrial network links such as PROFINET.

To address this issue, we introduce an embedded linear regression calibration module that runs on the PLC platform, integrated with a secondary STM32F407 for data logging and a Siemens S7-1500 for real-time control. The proposed system is designed to be conservative with CPU load, verifiable against safety interlocks, and repeatable across maintenance windows. Contributions include:
- A deployable linear regression calibration procedure for encoder angle-to-position mapping designed for PLC execution, evaluated on a physical 3-DoF arm at Universitas Gadjah Mada WTP testbed.
- A software and network architecture integrating the PLC, STM32 data logger, and SCADA with OPC-UA/PROFINET links, including measured scan-cycle timings and communication latencies.
- Experimental validation demonstrating RMSE reduction from 3.60 mm to 1.20 mm and accuracy improvement to 95.4% while lowering median latency to 12.3 ms.
- Practical discussion of safety integration (emergency stop, torque limits), limitations of linear calibration in highly non-linear regimes, and recommended deployment guidelines for municipal WTP environments.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II places the work in context by reviewing robotics calibration, PLC-based controllers, and industrial network integration. Section III details the system design and methodology including mechanical kinematics, regression formulation, and PLC implementation. Section IV presents experimental protocols and results obtained on the UGM WTP testbed, including ablation and endurance tests. Section V concludes the paper and outlines directions for field trials and enhancements to non-linear calibration.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section organizes prior work into three strands: calibration and parameter identification for robotic arms, PLC-based industrial control and integration, and safety-aware deployment in chemical handling and water treatment contexts. Each subsection highlights concrete limitations and distinctions relative to our approach.

content.text: Robotic arm calibration has a long history from classical Denavit-Hartenberg parameter tuning to modern machine learning approaches. Early geometric calibration methods focused on minimizing forward kinematics residuals by adjusting link lengths and joint offsets [7]. Subsequent work used system identification with extended Kalman filters to combine encoder and inertial measurements, improving dynamic performance for high-speed manipulators [8][9]. Recent data-driven strategies employ neural networks to correct encoder non-linearities or measure cable stretch in continuum manipulators [10][11]. However, neural methods often require substantial compute and are sensitive to domain shift; these traits complicate certification and deterministic deployment in PLC-centered plants [12]. Linear regression and polynomial compensation remain attractive because they admit closed-form solutions and can be scheduled during maintenance windows with predictable CPU cost [13]. In addition, linear models are transparent and amenable to formal verification of bounds, which reduces operational risk in chemical dosing applications.

content.text: Fig. 1 summarizes the taxonomy and motivates our selection of a linear regression block: closed-form solvability, small memory footprint, and deterministic execution. The illustration contextualizes our method relative to EKF-based observers [8] and neural corrections [10], and it transitions into discussion of PLC constraints in the next subsection.

Industrial controllers such as Siemens S7-series and Rockwell ControlLogix dominate chemical process automation due to long-term support, certified I/O modules, and standardized programming languages (IEC 61131-3). Recent studies show these platforms can host advanced algorithms if computational and scan-cycle constraints are respected [5][14]. Communication via PROFINET, OPC-UA, and MQTT are common in modern WTPs; works such as [15] and [16] evaluate deterministic packet delivery and scan-cycle interactions for motion control. A practical differentiation for our design is the requirement to guarantee safety interlock checks before any actuator command is issued, which demands the calibration update be integrated as a non-critical background task or as an atomic update that is switched in only when interlocks are satisfied. Prior work on PLC offloading to auxiliary microcontrollers for logging and heavy computation is instructive, yet many implementations do not demonstrate full integration with a production SCADA stack [17]. Our approach follows the dual-processor pattern: offload data collection and archival to an STM32F407 while keeping the regression routine minimal enough to run on the S7-1500 under a scheduled maintenance scan window.

This subsection references [5][14][15][16][17] to show the state of practice and contrasts the present work by explicitly measuring $T_{\mathrm{scan}}$ and the effect of calibration switch-in on control latency.

section2c.title: Chemical Handling and Safety in Water Treatment

content.text: Automation in chemical dosing introduces operational hazards including over-dosing, spills, and cross-contamination. Standards and best practices for dosing systems emphasize fail-safe shutoffs, redundant measurements, and event logging for traceability [18][19]. Field studies in municipal WTPs highlight that integration complexity, not algorithmic novelty, is the frequent cause of delayed deployment [20]. Particular to robotic arms, mechanical design choices (material compatibility, seals, and wetted components) and software interlocks for dosing sequences are crucial; several documented incidents underscore the need for conservative dosing limits and operator override paths [21]. The current study situates itself in this operationally constrained environment: calibration must not disable safety checks, and any automatic parameter update is gated by a review step visible on the HMI.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section presents the complete design: mechanical kinematics for the 3-DoF arm, the linear regression calibration formulation, PLC implementation details, and the communication/integration pipeline. The architecture balances computational cost and deterministic timing while preserving safety interlocks and operator visibility.

content.text: The hardware-software architecture centers on a Siemens S7-1500 PLC as the authoritative motion controller and safety arbiter. An STM32F407 acts as a data-logger and auxiliary computation node that collects high-frequency encoder and IMU samples for off-line analysis. Servo amplifiers drive three joint actuators (J1, J2, J3) with built-in current sensing. Communication uses PROFINET/CAT6 for deterministic real-time signals and OPC-UA to the SCADA server for logging and operator-level configuration. The HMI provides an operator interface for calibration routine control, operator sign-off, and emergency stop acknowledgement. The architecture is illustrated in Fig. 2, and the PLC ladder logic encapsulates a calibration 'Apply' bit which atomically replaces encoder-to-angle mapping only when safety conditions are met.

The system design emphasizes bounded compute in the PLC: heavy-data operations such as sample aggregation and initial regression prototyping are performed on the STM32F407 and on a maintenance laptop when needed. The PLC executes only the final 1-D linear compensation per joint in periodic cycles to preserve determinism $T_{\mathrm{scan}}$.

content.text: Equation (1) shows the homogeneous transformation for a single-link frame used in the forward kinematics chain. For the 3-DoF arm we compute end-effector pose by successive multiplies of transforms $T_1 T_2 T_3$. The joint vector $q = [\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3]^T$ maps to Cartesian end-effector coordinates $x= f(q)$ via the combined transforms. The Jacobian $J(q)$ is used for sensitivity analysis and for computing small corrections in joint space when the regression-corrected angles are applied. This modular approach keeps on-line kinematics simple so the PLC can meet the 10 ms control loop without heavy matrix inversion.

The physical rig used in this study is installed in the Universitas Gadjah Mada WTP laboratory. The manipulator is a custom aluminum 3-DoF serial arm with a 650 mm maximum reach and brushed stainless steel end-effector for chemical compatibility. Joint actuators are industrial servos coupled with absolute encoders. The control stack is centered on a Siemens S7-1500 CPU 1516-3 PN/DP, three Yaskawa-type servo amplifiers with 48V DC motor bus, and an STM32F407 evaluation board used for data-logging and offline computation. The HMI is a 10.1 inch touchscreen running WinCC Basic connected via PROFINET. E-stop circuits and current-limited relays are hardwired to the PLC safety I/O. Power is supplied by a 48V DC redundant bus with an isolated 24V DC control supply.

Table I enumerates the principal hardware components. The encoder CPR and motor bus voltage directly affect achievable joint resolution and torque, and thus they influence the achievable RMSE after calibration. The STM32F407 operates at 168 MHz and stores raw sample buffers (N=500 per calibration run) while offloading heavy file transfers to an SD card to avoid increasing $T_{\mathrm{scan}}$ on the PLC.

content.text: We treat calibration as a mapping from raw encoder-derived joint angles to corrected joint angles that minimize Cartesian displacement errors. Let the dataset be $\{x_i,y_i\}_{i=1}^{N}$ where $x_i\in \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are encoder features (raw angles, temperature, timestamp) and $y_i\in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ are target Cartesian coordinates measured by a reference jig. We use a batch linear regression per Cartesian axis due to its closed-form solution and predictable computational cost on the PLC. The linear model for one axis is $y = X\theta + \varepsilon$, where $X$ includes a bias column and measured features. Training occurs during a maintenance window and the resulting $\theta$ is stored as PLC variables accessible to ladder logic.

Equation (2) presents the normal equation used for closed-form least-squares estimation. On the STM32F407 and a maintenance laptop we compute (2) using double precision; the PLC stores the resulting parameters with sufficient fixed-point scaling to evaluate $x^{T}\theta$ every control cycle. The least-squares cost function minimized is written as

where $N$ is the number of calibration samples. We validate the linearity assumption by examining residuals and $R^2$ during training. If $R^2$ falls below a set threshold (0.92 in our deployment), the system warns operators and suggests a richer model or mechanical inspection. In run-time the PLC computes corrected joint angles $\theta_{\mathrm{corr}} = x^{T}\theta$ and feeds them to inverse kinematics and the PID motion controller. The inner servo loop uses a discrete PID with gains $K_p$, $K_i$, $K_d$ and a sampling period $T_s=10$ ms:

content.text: Equation (4) is implemented as a standard IEC 61131-3 PID function block on the S7-1500. The regression mapping reduces systematic bias so the PID acts primarily on higher frequency disturbances. To evaluate accuracy we compute the root-mean-square error $\mathrm{RMSE}$ across $N$ reference points:

The RMSE metric is used throughout the experiments to quantify geometric accuracy. Fig. 4 presents the algorithm flowchart, showing data acquisition, regressions, validation, and atomic update steps. The atomic update is implemented as a ladder logic rung that only copies a calibration table into active mapping when the 'Apply' bit is set and safety inputs indicate normal status.

content.text: Communication design must balance determinism and visibility. PROFINET is used for real-time cyclic exchange between the S7-1500 PLC and servo amplifiers and for HMI updates at 10 Hz. SCADA telemetry uses OPC-UA for event logging and MQTT for low-frequency external analytics. The STM32F407 collects raw samples at 50 Hz over a dedicated UART and writes archival records to SD card and to the SCADA server via an OPC-UA gateway during off-peak windows. The calibration training pipeline moves data to a maintenance laptop for initial analysis and then the final $\theta$ parameters are uploaded back to the PLC via secured OPC-UA with operator confirmation. Fig. 5 diagrams the communication topology including VLAN segmentation.

We measure each term experimentally in Section IV to ensure that introducing the calibration parameter application step does not push $T_{\mathrm{scan}}$ past safety thresholds. If $T_{\mathrm{exec}}$ increases temporarily during an atomic update, the PLC design defers non-critical tasks or executes the update within a scheduled maintenance scan slot.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: We conducted experiments on the UGM WTP testbed to evaluate calibration accuracy, latency, and endurance. The protocol includes baseline measurement, regression training with N=500 samples, validation across 200 unseen points, and endurance runs of 10,000 cycles to assess drift.

content.text: Experiments were performed in the UGM WTP robotics lab between February and March 2025. The rig includes the 3-DoF arm on a stainless steel base adjacent to a 500 L dosing tank. Reference positions were collected using a calibrated measurement jig with 0.5 mm repeatability. Sampling rate during acquisition was 50 Hz and each calibration run collected N=500 labeled samples by commanding the arm to a pseudo-random sequence of joint angles covering the reachable workspace uniformly. Environmental temperature ranged from 23.1 to 24.8 degC during runs and was logged to ensure temperature dependency was observed. The PLC scan period was nominally 10 ms prior to modifications.

section4b.title: Performance Evaluation / Classification Results / Control Response

content.text: We report positional accuracy, RMSE, and control latency. Baseline measurements used factory encoder mappings and tuned PID gains. After collecting N=500 samples, linear regression parameters (Equation (2)) were computed off-line and transferred to the PLC. Validation consisted of commanding 200 unseen Cartesian targets and measuring the Euclidean error. The baseline RMSE was 3.60 mm and after applying the regression mapping it dropped to 1.20 mm, representing a 66.7% reduction in geometric error. Positional accuracy, defined as the percentage of validation points within a 2.0 mm tolerance, improved from 89.2% to 95.4%. Median control latency measured end-to-end (command to measured motion update) reduced from 45.3 ms to 12.3 ms because calibration reduced corrective oscillations and therefore shortened settling times.

Table III aggregates the primary performance metrics and matches the values used in the comparison chart of Fig. 7. To compute classification-style accuracy we used a tolerance threshold and counted successful points. The RMSE and latency improvements are interdependent: a better feedforward mapping reduces large corrective PID actions, which reduces energy dissipation and settling time. We plot learning curves in Fig. 6 and report the loss function (Equation (3)) decreasing to a steady plateau consistent with adequate model capacity for the sampled workspace.

For continuous control metrics such as latency we report median and 95th percentile to capture occasional jitter. Our median latency of 12.3 ms is measured from HMI command issuance to encoder-confirmed steady-state position and includes network propagation and PLC execution time.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods / Ablation Study

content.text: We compared the proposed method against baseline PID, PID with model-based calibration (analytical kinematic parameter tuning), and a literature-reported approach (Method A) that uses sensor fusion with an EKF. The ablation study measured the effect of removing temperature as a regression feature and of halving the regression dataset to N=250. Omitting temperature increased RMSE from 1.20 mm to 1.35 mm, indicating modest thermal sensitivity across the 1.7 degC observed range. Reducing samples to N=250 increased RMSE to 1.45 mm and reduced accuracy to 93.2%, showing that sample coverage matters. Compared to the EKF-based Method A, our approach achieves similar accuracy with lower implementation complexity and better determinism on PLC hardware.

content.text: Table IV and Fig. 8 demonstrate that the proposed algorithm is competitive with more complex methods but runs on industrial PLC hardware. The ablation study highlights sample size and temperature as practical levers. One limitation is that highly non-linear joint behavior (for example, large cable stretch under heavy loads) would exceed the expressive capacity of a linear model; in such cases polynomial regression or piecewise linear mapping may be necessary.

Endurance tests consisted of 10,000 repetitive dosing cycles over five days with periodic calibration checks every 2,000 cycles. We monitored encoder drift, temperature, current draw, and error counts. Drift remained below 0.4 mm over 10,000 cycles. A total of two minor communication timeouts were recorded caused by an unrelated network switch and are not attributable to calibration logic. Chemical exposure tests used 0.1 mol/L solutions and the wetted parts showed no visible degradation after the test period. The PLC maintained $T_{\mathrm{scan}}$ below 12 ms throughout; during atomic calibration apply events the max observed $T_{\mathrm{scan}}$ was 18 ms but occurred during scheduled maintenance windows.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: This paper presented a deployable linear regression-based calibration workflow for a PLC-controlled 3-DoF robotic arm used in chemical handling at a water treatment plant. The implementation on a Siemens S7-1500 PLC with an STM32F407 data logger offers a pragmatic pathway for municipal operators to improve dosing accuracy without replacing the existing control infrastructure. Key results include a reduction in RMSE from 3.60 mm to 1.20 mm, a positional accuracy increase to 95.4%, and a reduction in median control latency to 12.3 ms. We demonstrated that the calibration procedure can be safely integrated into PLC safety logic with atomic parameter updates that occur only when interlocks are satisfied.

Despite these gains, limitations remain. Linear regression assumes approximately linear residuals across the sampled workspace; in regimes with pronounced non-linearities due to cable stretch, gear backlash, or large thermal gradients, richer models may be required. We observed modest thermal sensitivity across 1.7 °C, which suggests periodic recalibration or temperature-compensated features should be considered for continuous deployment. Another constraint is operator workflow: scheduling maintenance window executions for regression updates requires coordination with plant operations to avoid dosing interruptions.

Future work includes three specific directions. First, extend the method to piecewise-linear or low-order polynomial regression that retains closed-form solution properties while handling moderate non-linearity. Second, implement on-line recursive least squares with forgetting factor on the STM32F407 to permit incremental adaptation during low-risk operational periods. Third, conduct full field trials at an operating municipal WTP to evaluate month-long drift characteristics and to validate safety procedures under real operational loads. These steps will move the technique from laboratory validation toward field-hardened deployment.
